title: Capstone: measuring what a wrong guess costs
objective: By the end of this capstone you can explain why a pipeline must guess at every branch, measure the cost of guessing wrongly on your own machine, and recognise when that cost has been removed rather than paid.

blocks.text: Two hazards remain from the pipeline lesson's warning, and both were about data. This one is about control: the processor does not know which instruction comes next.

blocks.caption: A branch decides the next address, and it decides it late
lines: beq  x5, x6, target      # take the branch only if x5 equals x6
add  x9, x1, x2          # is this the next instruction, or is it not?
cycle:       1     2     3     4     5
beq        | IF  | ID  | EX  | MEM | WB  |
the comparison finishes here, cycle 3
But the fetch stage needed an address in cycle 2 — it cannot sit idle.
Every cycle it does not fetch is a cycle of the pipeline left empty.

blocks.title: Waiting is not an option, so the processor guesses
blocks.text: About one instruction in five or six is a branch. If the pipeline stopped and waited at each one, the overlap that pipelining bought would be lost several times per hundred instructions. So the fetch stage picks a direction and continues fetching. When the branch resolves and the guess was right, nothing was lost. When it was wrong, every instruction fetched since the branch is discarded and fetching restarts at the correct address.

headers: Roughly how often it is right
rows: Always not-taken
Fetch the next instruction in order
About half, for typical code
Backwards taken, forwards not
A backwards branch is probably a loop
Good for loops, poor elsewhere
One-bit history
Predict what this branch did last time
Wrong twice per loop: on entry and on exit
Two-bit saturating
Needs two wrong guesses to change its mind
Wrong once per loop instead of twice
Correlating / pattern
Uses the outcomes of recent branches as context
High, when the pattern is learnable

blocks.text: The progression down that table is one idea repeated: use more history. A loop that runs a thousand times is trivially predictable, and the two-bit scheme exists precisely so that the single not-taken exit does not flip the prediction for the next entry. What no amount of history helps with is a branch whose direction genuinely depends on unpredictable data — and that is what the measurement below constructs.

Sum the elements of an array that exceed a threshold. Run it on the same data twice: once in random order, once sorted. The arithmetic, the element count and the answer are identical. Only the predictability of the branch differs — sorted data means the condition is false for a long run and then true for a long run, which any history-based predictor learns immediately.

blocks.caption: Build it yourself
lines: static int data[N];
long sum_branch(void) {
long s = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < REP; r++)
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
if (data[i] >= 128) s += data[i];      /* the branch under test */
return s;
/* fill data with values 0..255 from a simple generator, time sum_branch(),
then qsort the array, time it again, and print both. */

blocks.caption: Measured on an Apple M-series processor, interleaved runs, best of five
lines: 1,048,576 elements x 64 passes, identical data, identical arithmetic,
identical element count. The only difference is the order of the elements.
compiled with -O0 (the branch is really executed):
unsorted : 0.560 s
sorted   : 0.081 s
ratio    : 6.91x
compiled with -O2 (the compiler removed the branch entirely):
unsorted : 0.008 s
sorted   : 0.008 s
ratio    : 1.00x

blocks.text: Reading the second half of that result

At -O0 the branch is genuinely executed and the answer is unambiguous: unpredictable data cost almost seven times as much as predictable data, for identical work. That is the misprediction penalty made visible. At -O2 the difference vanished exactly — 1.00x — and the temptation is to conclude that the optimiser 'made both cases fast'. Check the assembly instead of assuming.

blocks.caption: What -O2 actually produced
lines: $ cc -O2 -S -o - branch.c | sed -n '/_sum_branch:/,/ret/p'
cmgt.4s   v3, v1, v2        # compare four values at once, produce a mask
and.16b   v4, v1, v3        # keep the ones that passed, zero the rest
uaddw.2d  v5, v5, v4        # add them all in, including the zeros
/* There is no conditional branch in the loop body at all. The comparison
became a mask and the addition became unconditional: values that failed
the test contribute zero. Four elements per instruction, no prediction
involved, and therefore nothing to mispredict. */

blocks.title: The optimiser did not predict better; it removed the thing being predicted
blocks.text: A conditional branch was replaced by a comparison producing a mask and an unconditional addition. Nothing is guessed, so nothing can be guessed wrongly, and the two orderings become indistinguishable — which is exactly the 1.00x that was measured. This is the general technique called branchless or predicated code, and the same idea appears as a conditional-move instruction in the assembly course. It is also why a benchmark of branch prediction must be checked at the optimisation level it was compiled at.

blocks.title: A measurement discipline worth keeping
blocks.text: A first attempt at this experiment ran unsorted then sorted, once, at -O2 and reported 1.71x — a plausible-looking number that was pure ordering artifact from the first timed run. Interleaving the two cases and taking the best of five runs gave 1.00x, repeatedly and exactly. When a performance number is small and you have run each case once, you have measured your measurement setup, not the machine.

items: Build the program above and measure at -O0 and at -O2
Interleave the sorted and unsorted cases and repeat at least five times, reporting the best of each
Inspect the -O2 assembly and decide for yourself whether a branch is still there
Replace the branch with an explicit branchless form and measure it at -O0
Explain each of the four numbers in one sentence

blocks.caption: The branchless form to compare against
lines: /* with a branch */
if (data[i] >= 128) s += data[i];
/* without: the comparison produces 0 or 1, and the multiply makes
the addition unconditional */
s += data[i] * (data[i] >= 128);
/* Or with an explicit mask, which is closer to what the vectoriser did:
int m = -(data[i] >= 128);      // 0 or all-ones
s += data[i] & m;
Measure at -O0, where the compiler is not rewriting your code, so you
can see what the transformation is worth by itself. */

blocks.text: What you should be able to say at the end

headers: The answer your own numbers support
rows: Why must a processor guess at a branch?
The fetch stage needs an address several cycles before the branch resolves
What does a wrong guess cost?
Everything fetched since the branch, discarded — measured at 6.91x on unpredictable data
Why did sorting help?
It made the condition's outcome a long run of one answer, which a history-based predictor learns immediately
Why did -O2 make the difference disappear?
It removed the branch, replacing it with a mask and an unconditional add
When is branchless code worth writing?
When the condition is genuinely unpredictable and the work on both sides is cheap

blocks.text: That last row is the practical rule, and it has a real limit: branchless code does the work of both sides every time. When one side is expensive or has an effect, doing it unconditionally is either slower or wrong. The transformation pays only when the branch is unpredictable and both sides are cheap — which is precisely the case the experiment constructed, and precisely why it is not a general recommendation.

blocks.title: Where this connects
blocks.text: The deep-pipeline calculation in the pipeline lesson asked you to include a misprediction penalty and found the deeper design losing. You have now measured the phenomenon that calculation was about. The security course's treatment of speculative-execution attacks starts from the same mechanism: the processor really does execute the instructions after a branch before knowing whether it should have, and the effects of that work do not all disappear when it is discarded.

blocks.title: Extend the experiment
steps: Change the threshold from 128 to 0 so the condition is always true, and measure
Change it to 256 so the condition is always false, and measure
Explain why both extremes are as fast as the sorted case
Make the condition depend on i % 2 and measure — is an alternating pattern predictable?
Make it depend on i % 3, then a pattern of period 7, and find where prediction fails
Report the shortest repeating pattern your machine could not predict
Compare that number with what the table above says about correlating predictors
blocks.expected: Both constant conditions as fast as sorted, alternating patterns predicted well, and a period beyond which the predictor loses. The period where it fails is a direct measurement of how much branch history your processor keeps — a hardware property you established without any documentation, using only a loop and a clock.

cheatsheet: A control hazard: the next address is not known until the branch resolves
The fetch stage cannot wait, so it guesses and continues fetching
A wrong guess discards everything fetched since the branch
Predictors improve by using more history: one-bit, two-bit saturating, correlating
Two-bit exists so a loop's single exit does not flip the prediction for the next entry
Measured at -O0: unpredictable data cost 6.91x predictable data for identical work
Measured at -O2: exactly 1.00x, because the compiler replaced the branch with a mask
Branchless code does both sides' work every time — only worth it when both are cheap
One timed run per case measures your setup; interleave and take the best of several
Speculative-execution attacks start from this same mechanism

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a pipelined processor guess a branch direction instead of waiting?

choices.A: Branches are rare enough that waiting for them is cheap
choices.D: Fetch needs the address before the branch resolves

checkpoint.explanation: About one instruction in five or six is a branch. Stopping at each one would give back most of what pipelining bought. Every cycle spent not fetching leaves the pipeline empty.

checkpoint.prompt: Sorting the array made the same loop 6.91x faster at -O0. Why?

choices.A: Sorted data has better cache locality
choices.B: Sorting turned the condition into a long run of false followed by a long run of true
choices.D: The sum is easier to compute on sorted data

checkpoint.explanation: A history-based predictor learns immediately. Identical elements, identical arithmetic, identical answer. Only the predictability of the branch changed, so only misprediction can explain the difference.

checkpoint.prompt: At -O2 the sorted and unsorted cases took exactly the same time. What does the assembly show happened?

choices.A: The predictor got better with optimisation
choices.D: The conditional branch was replaced by a comparison producing a mask and an unconditional add

checkpoint.explanation: There is nothing to predict. cmgt produces the mask, and produces the sum unconditionally with failing elements contributing zero. No branch means no misprediction, hence exactly 1.00x.

checkpoint.prompt: When is rewriting a branch into branchless form a bad idea?

choices.A: When the branch is predictable, or when one side is expensive or has an effect, since branchless code performs both sides every time
choices.C: It is never a bad idea

checkpoint.explanation: A well-predicted branch already costs almost nothing, so removing it gains nothing while adding the other side's work. And a side with an effect cannot be executed unconditionally at all.
